mcqs.question: Why does using a minimal base image (like a distroless image) reduce a container's vulnerability surface compared to a full OS base image?
options: It has fewer installed packages overall, so there are fewer pieces of software that could carry a known CVE in the first place
It automatically encrypts all data the application writes to disk
It prevents the application's own code from ever containing a vulnerability
It replaces the need for image scanning entirely
mcqs.explanation: Fewer packages means fewer places a known vulnerability can hide, including in packages the application never actually uses — that's the entire mechanism. A minimal image doesn't add encryption, doesn't protect against vulnerabilities in the application's own code, and scanning is still needed for whatever packages remain.

mcqs.question: An application container runs as root with a writable root filesystem. If an attacker achieves code execution through an application vulnerability, what does this configuration specifically make easier for them?
options: It hands the attacker root privileges inside the container and lets them write/persist files, both of which make further exploitation (including attempting a container breakout) easier
It only affects performance, not what the attacker can do post-compromise
It prevents the attacker from reading any files at all
Nothing — running as root inside a container has no security implication since the container is isolated from the host
mcqs.explanation: Root access and write ability inside the container are exactly the capabilities an attacker needs to escalate further or persist — restricting both is cheap, real hardening. Container isolation doesn't neutralize this risk, the configuration is a security concern rather than a performance one, and it doesn't prevent reading files.

mcqs.question: A pod is deployed without explicitly configuring a ServiceAccount or RBAC. What determines what that pod's workload can do against the Kubernetes API?
options: The pod automatically has no access to the Kubernetes API at all unless RBAC is explicitly configured
Kubernetes requires every pod to specify RBAC or it will fail to schedule
RBAC only applies to human users logging into the cluster, never to pods
It runs under the cluster's default ServiceAccount, whose permissions may be broader than the workload actually needs if RBAC hasn't been deliberately scoped
mcqs.explanation: Every pod runs as some ServiceAccount, defaulting to the cluster's `default` one if nothing else is set — and that default can carry more permission than a given workload needs unless someone deliberately scopes it, which is exactly the least-privilege gap this slide covers. Pods aren't blocked from the API by default, aren't required to specify RBAC to schedule, and RBAC absolutely applies to ServiceAccounts, not just human users.

mcqs.question: A Kubernetes cluster has no NetworkPolicy resources defined anywhere. What does that mean for pod-to-pod traffic?
options: Traffic between pods requires mutual TLS by default in every Kubernetes distribution
Any pod can reach any other pod, on any port, across any namespace — the network is fully flat until a policy explicitly restricts it
Kubernetes automatically applies default-deny between namespaces even without any policy defined
Pods can only communicate within their own namespace by default
mcqs.explanation: Kubernetes networking is flat by default — no NetworkPolicy means no restriction, so any pod can reach any other pod regardless of namespace, which is exactly why writing default-deny policies is a deliberate step someone has to take. There's no built-in mTLS or cross-namespace default-deny without configuring it, and namespace boundaries alone don't restrict network reachability.

mcqs.question: A team stores a database password in a Kubernetes Secret object and considers it encrypted because the value isn't shown in plaintext when viewed in some tools. Is this accurate?
options: Yes, Kubernetes Secrets are always encrypted using a cluster-wide key by default
No — Kubernetes Secret values are base64-encoded by default, a reversible encoding requiring no key, not encrypted; encryption at rest for etcd is a separate, explicitly configured feature
Yes, but only if the Secret is created through the kubectl CLI rather than a manifest file
No — Kubernetes Secrets cannot store passwords at all, only certificates
mcqs.explanation: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption — no key is needed to reverse it, so anyone with API or etcd access can trivially recover the value unless etcd encryption at rest is separately enabled. Secrets aren't encrypted by default regardless of creation method, and they can absolutely store arbitrary values including passwords.

mcqs.question: A CI pipeline mounts the host's Docker socket into a build container so the build job can create and run its own containers. What risk does this specifically introduce?
options: It only affects the speed of the build, not its security
It has no risk as long as the build container itself runs as a non-root user

The build container gets direct control over the host's container runtime and can create a new container that mounts the host's root filesystem, which is a straightforward path to full host compromise
It prevents the build container from creating any new containers at all, breaking Docker-in-Docker workflows
mcqs.explanation: The Docker socket is a direct control channel to the host's runtime — a container with access to it can spin up a new container with whatever host mounts and privileges it chooses, which is a real, well-documented breakout path, not a theoretical one. Running as non-root inside the build container doesn't neutralize this because the socket itself grants host-level control, this is a security issue rather than merely a performance one, and mounting the socket is precisely what enables Docker-in-Docker workflows (that's the risk, not the absence of it).
